title: A Photograph (Poem, Hornbill)
tagline: Shirley Toulson’s three-stanza lyric: a photograph, a mother’s laughter, and the silence that grief cannot speak through.

overview.intro: A poem of twenty-odd lines and three sections, A Photograph moves across three times: the mother’s childhood at the sea, her laughter years later over the album, and the poet’s present, from which the mother has gone. The unit studies how the poem uses the photograph as an object to hold three periods at once, how the sea functions as the one thing that seems to stay while everything human changes, and how the final line converts an image into an emotion.

learningOutcomes: Summarise the movement of the three stanzas across three times.
Explain the contrast between the unchanging sea and the transient human figures.
Account for the effect of the mother’s laughter in the second stanza.
Interpret the final line and the poem’s treatment of loss.
Answer extract questions on images and sound patterns in the poem.

learn.title: The three sections: three times, one object

blocks.text: The first section describes the photograph itself. The mother, who would have been about twelve, is paddling in the sea with her cousins Betty and Dolly, and the picture is mounted on cardboard — a physical detail that fixes the poem in an album rather than in memory alone. The poet’s comment is reserved for the last two lines of the stanza: the sea appears to have washed the girls’ feet apparently forever, but the feet are transient. The observation is small and exact, and it sets the poem’s theme without announcing it: what looks permanent in the picture is the water, and what is actually passing is the human figure.

The second section moves to a later time, when the mother, grown, looks at the same photograph and laughs. Her laughter is described as all the life the photograph can hold — that is, the picture cannot contain her, only provoke her. The cousins are already mentioned as having later become mothers themselves, so the middle section quietly multiplies the distance travelled: the girl in the picture has become a woman who laughs at her own youth, and the people with her have made families of their own. The third section then takes the last step: the mother has been dead for years, the poet is left holding the album, and the poem ends not with a memory but with a statement about silence.

learn.title: The sea, the cardboard and the images that carry meaning

blocks.text: The sea is the poem’s structural device. In the picture it looks as though it will wash the girls’ feet forever, which is exactly the illusion a photograph offers: a moment arrested and therefore made to seem permanent. The adjective transient applied to the feet states the truth beneath the illusion, and the poet does not moralise over it because the contrast has already done the work. The second image is the cardboard on which the photograph is mounted — a domestic object, slightly absurd in its formality, which gives the poem its texture of an album handled over years.

The third image is silence, and it arrives as the poem’s conclusion. Silence in the first two sections is merely the absence of noise in a still picture; in the final stanza it becomes the state of a bereaved person for whom language has run out. The pun in “its silence silences” — the silence of the photograph and of the sea-picture silencing the poet — is the poem’s one rhetorical flourish, and it earns its place because everything before it has been stated quietly. Examination answers should note that the image of the sea returns in the last stanza as “the silence of hearts”, so the object and the grief are held in the same frame.

items: The sea looks permanent in the picture; the human feet are transient.
The cardboard mount gives the poem its album texture.
The mother’s laughter is the life the photograph cannot contain.
The cousins becoming mothers quietly measures the years passed.
Silence moves from stillness in a picture to grief beyond speech.

learn.title: Sound, form and the economy of the poem

blocks.text: The poem is written in free verse of three irregular stanzas, and its sound patterning is subtle rather than conspicuous. The long vowels of “laughter” and the soft consonants of “silence” slow the reading at the poem’s two emotional points, and the alliteration of “washed” and “well” in the first stanza gives the sea’s sentence its motion. What is more striking is the poem’s economy: it never names grief, never describes the mother’s illness or death, and never addresses her directly, which is unusual for a elegy and is precisely why the last line lands.

For examination purposes the poem supports two standard questions. The first is about the movement of time, which is answered with the three sections and their dates implied. The second is about images — sea, feet, cardboard, laughter, silence — which should each be explained for what it contributes rather than quoted. A common loss of marks comes from reading the poem as nostalgia alone; its second half is about bereavement, and the distinction should appear in any answer that claims more than three lines.

items.note: The sea’s apparent permanence set against the briefness of the human figure.
The photograph’s stillness converted into the poet’s inability to speak.

blocks.text: Extract questions usually isolate one of the two turning lines — the transient feet or the silence — and ask for effect. The reliable shape of the answer is: state the literal meaning in the picture, then the figurative meaning, then the emotional consequence for the poet, all in three or four sentences. For example, on the transient feet: the sea in the photograph seems to wash them forever; in life the girls have aged and the mother has died; therefore the picture, which appears to fix a moment, in fact measures its passing.

Longer questions ask about the poem’s treatment of time or memory, and here the answer should follow the sequence of the three sections and then add the argument: memory is unreliable in what it retains but honest in what it cannot recover, and the poem’s restraint is the formal equivalent of that honesty. The poet does not sentimentalise, does not apostrophise the dead mother, and ends on an image rather than a declaration — which is the most a poem can honestly do with a bereavement it did not dramatise.

keyPoints: The poem has three sections moving across three different times.
The mother is about twelve in the photograph, with cousins Betty and Dolly.
The sea seems to wash the girls’ feet forever; their feet are transient.
The photograph is mounted on cardboard in a family album.
In the second section the grown mother laughs at the picture.
Her cousins later become mothers, quietly measuring the years.
In the third section the mother has been dead for years.
The poem never names grief or describes the mother’s death.
The closing line, its silence silences, converts an image into an emotion.

questions.prompt: How does the poem move through three different times?
questions.answer: The first section is set in the mother’s childhood: a photograph of her at about twelve, paddling in the sea with her cousins, over which the poet comments that the sea seems to wash their feet forever although their feet are transient. The second section moves to the mother’s adulthood, when she looks at the same photograph and laughs, and the mention of her cousins having become mothers quietly marks the years that have passed. The third section is the poet’s present: the mother has been dead for years, the poet is left with the photograph, and the poem ends on silence rather than on memory. One photograph therefore holds three periods, and each section measures what has changed while the object stays the same.
questions.explanation: The three sections must be named with what each contributes to the poem’s movement.

questions.prompt: What is the significance of the sea in the poem?
questions.answer: The sea appears in the first section as the setting of the picture, where it seems to have washed the girls’ feet forever, and the poet immediately sets against that appearance the transience of the feet themselves. The sea therefore embodies the illusion the photograph creates: a moment arrested looks permanent, while the people in it continue to age and, in the mother’s case, die. The sea returns in the final section through the silence of hearts, so the same element that stood for apparent permanence now stands for the depth of what cannot be expressed. In this way the image binds the poem together: it is present in the picture, absent from the poet’s present, and finally merged with the grief the poem will not name.
questions.explanation: The answer must treat the sea as a structural image across the poem, not merely as the setting.

questions.prompt: Explain the poem’s treatment of memory and time with close reference to its images.
questions.answer: The poem treats memory as something held by objects rather than generated by will: the poet does not summon her mother but handles an album, and the three sections of the poem are arranged around that object. The first section gives the picture its physicality — the cardboard mount, the cousins, the paddling — and then adds the observation that the sea appears to wash the girls’ feet forever while the feet are transient. That couplet contains the poem’s whole argument about time: the photograph fixes an appearance of permanence, and the viewer supplies the knowledge that everything in it has passed. The second section advances the argument by showing the photograph in use: the grown mother laughs at her own childhood, which means the picture no longer depicts her but provokes her, and the mention of the cousins becoming mothers measures further distance without a date. The third section takes the final step, and the poem refuses to dramatise it — there is no deathbed, no tears, no address to the dead — because the point is not the event but the condition that follows. Memory, on this account, is reliable about objects and unreliable about comfort: the album preserves the face and cannot restore the person, and the closing silence names the gap. The images carry this consistently — the sea that seems permanent, the cardboard that ages, the laughter that the picture cannot hold, and the silence that finally occupies the place where speech was — so that the poem’s restraint is not reticence but accuracy about what memory can and cannot do.
questions.explanation: Full marks require the three sections traced through their images and a consistent argument about what memory preserves and what it cannot.

questions.prompt: Is the poem primarily about nostalgia, or about loss? Answer with evidence from the whole text.
questions.answer: The case for nostalgia rests on the first two sections, which are warm and specific: the album, the cardboard mount, three girls paddling, the named cousins, and the mother’s laughter when she later looks at the picture. These details are the material of family reminiscence, and the poem’s gentle tone — its refusal to moralise, its domestic objects — invites a reading centred on affection for a vanished childhood. Read this far, the poem seems to be about how a photograph keeps the past available. The case for loss rests on the structure rather than on any single line. The poem has three sections and the third is not another memory but a change of state: the mother has been dead for years, and the poem’s last word belongs to silence rather than to laughter. The second section already prepares this by describing the laughter as all the photograph can hold, which implies that what is held is less than what was — the picture preserves a trace, not a life. The final pun converts the stillness of an image into the speechlessness of the bereaved, and the earlier remark that the girls’ feet are transient has already told the reader that every person in the picture is passing. On this reading nostalgia is the poem’s opening premise and loss is its subject: the warmth of the first two sections exists so that the silence of the third has something to silence. The balanced judgement, then, is that the two are stages rather than rivals — the poem begins in remembrance and ends in bereavement, and its craft lies in making the transition without a single statement of grief. The best answers will quote from all three sections and show the direction of movement, because quoting only the opening produces nostalgia and quoting only the ending produces a plainer elegy than the poem actually is.
questions.explanation: Full marks require evidence from all three sections, the structural argument about where the poem ends, and a judgement that names the movement rather than choosing one label arbitrarily.
